analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA power to force food recalls, inspect food plants on a risk schedule, and trace contaminated food to its source.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 283-142 on July 30, 2009, but the Senate committee it was sent to never acted, and the bill died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul how the FDA oversees the food supply. Food facilities would have to register each year and pay a fee, write hazard-analysis and food-safety plans, and put preventive controls in place. The FDA could order recalls, impose science-based safety standards for produce, inspect plants on a schedule matched to risk, trace contaminated food to its source, and certify imported food. Meat, poultry, and egg plants already inspected by the Agriculture Department, plus alcohol facilities, were exempted.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats: fewer foodborne illness outbreaks like the 2009 salmonella and E. coli events, faster recalls when contamination happens, clearer country-of-origin labels, and stronger scrutiny of imported food. Workers at food plants also gain whistleblower protection from retaliation for reporting unsafe conditions.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every food facility to run a hazard analysis, implement preventive controls, and keep a written food safety plan before shipping food [S3].
Gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority to order an immediate stop to distribution or a recall of contaminated food, rather than relying on voluntary company recalls [S2].
Sets a risk-based inspection schedule, with high-risk plants inspected at least every 6 to 12 months, and creates a dedicated corps of inspectors for foreign food facilities [S4].
Requires a tracing system that lets the FDA identify everyone who handled a contaminated food within about two business days, so outbreaks can be traced to their source [S4].
Requires annual registration and fees for food importers, import certifications, and country-of-origin labeling, tightening oversight of imported food [S3].
Protects employees from being discriminated against for reporting food safety violations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers, processors, and importers: a $500 annual registration fee per facility (capped at $175,000 per company per year), reinspection and recall fees, costs of safety plans, testing by accredited labs, and expanded civil and criminal penalties. Some of those costs would likely reach shoppers as slightly higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The $500 annual facility registration fee and compliance costs fall on food businesses, including smaller ones, and part of that cost would be passed to consumers in prices [S4].

Small and very small businesses get only two and three extra years, respectively, before the preventive-control requirements take effect, so the compliance burden on small producers is real even though the bill directs the Secretary to consider their impact [S4].
The registration fee authority sunsets after fiscal year 2014, so the funding stream for the new inspections was temporary by design [S3].

The bill treats food as adulterated if a facility delays, limits, or refuses an inspection, extends prison terms for food-safety offenses from one year to ten, and expands civil penalties — provisions critics saw as giving the agency heavy leverage over businesses [S3].
The bill exempts USDA-inspected meat, poultry, and egg plants and alcohol facilities entirely, so a large share of the food supply stays under the older, separate regulatory regime [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: modest fees and compliance costs for food companies, partly passed to shoppers, in exchange for mandatory recall power, risk-based inspections, and traceability that address recurring outbreaks of foodborne illness. The bill was drafted carefully — farm exemptions, small-business phase-ins, and USDA carve-outs — but its temporary fee structure was a real weakness. On balance the benefits to consumers outweighed the costs.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 283-142, but after it was sent to the Senate's Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in August 2009, the Senate never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Introduced on June 8, 2009, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which amended and reported it on July 29 [S6].
A first attempt to pass it under a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds vote failed 280-150 on July 29, with 127 of 178 voting Republicans opposed [S7].

Leadership brought it back the next day under a rule that barred amendments; a Republican motion to recommit failed 186-240, and the bill passed 283-142, with 229 of 255 voting Democrats in favor and 122 of 178 voting Republicans against [S9].
The Senate received the bill on August 3, 2009, and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where no further action appears in the record [S6].
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, with the bill never reaching a Senate vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food facilities avoided the registration fees and the new preventive-control, inspection, and traceability requirements while the bill sat in the Senate. Consumers did not get the bill's protections from this legislation, though food safety was later addressed by separate legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food firms that avoided fees and rules

for.name: John D. Dingell
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and shepherded it through House consideration, including raising a point of order against a Republican motion to recommit.

for.name: Henry Waxman
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: His committee marked up and reported the bill to the House floor.

against.name: 122 of 179 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage; 127 also voted no on the earlier two-thirds-vote attempt the day before.

against.name: Tom Harkin
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on August 3, 2009, and never reported it or brought it to the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

against.name: Grocery Manufacturers Association
against.role: Trade association for large food and beverage makers
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's annual registration fees and pushed for a lighter-touch alternative during the 2009 food safety debate.

sides.party_line_note: House passage was 229-20 among Democrats but 54-122 among Republicans, so nearly the whole Democratic caucus backed the bill while most Republicans opposed it; a similar split appeared on the failed fast-track vote the day before (230-23 D, 50-127 R) [S7] [S9].

industries.note: The bill imposed an annual $500 registration fee per facility (capped at $175,000 per company), mandatory hazard analysis and preventive controls, risk-based inspections, reinspection and recall fees, and mandatory recall authority — costs the industry lobbied against. The industry's interest in avoiding those costs ran against consumers' interest in safer food.

Importers would have to register annually, pay fees, submit to certification requirements, and face a dedicated FDA corps inspecting foreign facilities. Their interest in lighter border scrutiny ran against consumers' interest in safer imports.

The bill required food testing for import or export to be done by accredited laboratories and established an accreditation program, making accredited labs the mandatory channel for that testing. That mandate serves safety while guaranteeing labs a role.
The bill explicitly exempted alcohol-related facilities from nearly all its requirements, keeping wineries, breweries, and distilleries outside the new safety regime.

The bill exempted USDA-regulated meat, poultry, and egg products and the facilities that produce them, so those plants avoided the new FDA fees and controls. They already operate under mandatory continuous USDA inspection, so the carve-out preserved the existing regime rather than removing oversight.

Farms, restaurants, and retail food establishments were excluded from the facility definition, and farm-direct sales were exempted from tracing requirements, sparing small producers most of the bill's cost.
